1confirmation has invested in every Polymarket round ever and we keep doubling down.

We are a seed stage fund and investing late stage is not our mandate. Here’s why we broke our rules: 

- There’s a 100+ year history of people wanting skin in the game on things like politics and culture and the time to accelerate that is now in an AI world where the biggest problem young people have is knowing what’s true. Everyone is becoming a trader/investor, and a product that converts that energy into better information and more truth is truly unique.

- Polymarket is much more than sports and global. In the U.S. right now sports is all the rage. A better sportsbook is fine but it’s not the most enduring aspect of a prediction market business. Better information and more truth on politics, geopolitics and culture is the why and most young people you talk to IRL know that Polymarket is in a class of its own on this front even though that discourse here can get lost.

- The business is leveling up. I’ve seen a lot over the past 6 years and it’s far from perfect but the exec team in place now is exceptional, the US product is best in class and the revenue is making new highs. I have not loved the messaging about a token at times bc it’s always best to underpromise and overdeliver by quietly delivering value to users. But the idea that a token is dead is foolish.

- Shayne has a will to win like none other and is the most direct and transparent person I know. He’s just himself and authenticity wins.

text:
“我们真的在走向 AGI 吗？”
Google CEO Sundar Pichai 在彭博专访中的态度极其谨慎：“技术的演进速度令人震惊，但它正展现出一种诡异的断层——它能在复杂任务上突飞猛进，却会在极其低级的常识上摔跟头。”

很多团队以为做安全就是套 护栏层或前置过滤器。但 Pichai 提到的“连显而易见的事都做错”，暴露出当前自回归架构的死穴：推理不可控。

1 当模型可以在某些逻辑上展现超人能力、却在边界上发生灾难性幻觉时，任何“外挂式安全”在面对越狱注入、提示词攻击时都形同虚设。

2 完整访谈里隐藏着一个关键转变：Google 不再空谈 100% 的 对齐 而是在做工程降级隔离。

真正的安全必须依赖系统级沙箱、多智能体校验与确定性代码降级机制；

将不可控的黑盒概率输出，死死限制在可控的运行环境里。

3 为什么大厂对 AGI 节奏开始表现出冷思考？
因为防御成本远高于破坏成本。
合成假信息、供应链毒化、自动化漏洞挖掘的门槛无限趋近于零，而大厂每构筑一道安全基线，都需要在 CapEx、算力消耗和推理延迟上付出数倍代价。

4 越靠近 AGI，最大的技术天花板就越不是参数量或算力，而是可验证性

安全从来不是合规报告，而是系统面对失控时的降级底线。

quoted_text:
Anthropic is about to sell the public a trillion-dollar company controlled by 2 shares worth less than a penny.

And the people buying it will have almost no way to change anything that happens next.

I read the voting section of Anthropic's IPO filing, and I think it's the most one-sided deal ever offered to regular investors at this size:

There is exactly ONE Class F share. It belongs to an LLC owned by 7 of Anthropic's co-founders, and it carries 50.1% of all the votes.

There is exactly ONE Class T share. It belongs to Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, and it elects a majority of the board.

If Anthropic were ever liquidated, each of those 2 shares would get its par value of $0.00001.

The public gets Class A shares instead. And Anthropic's own filing says this structure may effectively eliminate their ability to influence important decisions, including a sale of the company.

So here's what that means for anyone who buys:

- They can't replace the board if the company stumbles, because the trust picks the majority and the founders hold half the vote.
- They can't push for a sale, even if someone offers a huge premium.
- They can't stop the board from putting the mission ahead of their money. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, so the board has to weigh shareholders against the long-term benefit of humanity.
- And they can't easily sue over it. Delaware law requires at least 2% of the shares or $2 million worth of stock to bring that kind of claim.

This isn't some far-off hypothetical either.

The filing warns that slowing AI development for safety may not maximize stockholder value. It also says Anthropic recently paused training a next-generation model for more than a month over safety and security concerns.

A public shareholder would've had zero say in that pause.

And here's the part I can't get past:

Each co-founder has pledged to give 80% of their Anthropic equity to charity. The Class F vote stays at 50.1% no matter how much stock they still own.

So the founders can give away most of their money and keep all of their control.

Dario Amodei told 60 Minutes last year that he's deeply uncomfortable with AI decisions being made by a few companies and a few people. When he was asked who elected him, he said no one.

Now his company's IPO hands 50.1% of the votes to 7 people, and he's one of them.

And guess who's being lined up to buy it?

Anthropic has weighed reserving 15% to 20% of the IPO for individual investors, according to Bloomberg. JPMorgan is leading the US retail push, and Citigroup is handling retail buyers in places like Japan, Britain and Canada.

The same filing warns that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

So regular people are being asked to buy a company that says its product could threaten humanity, with no real vote on how it's run.

Anthropic's answer is that this is the whole point. The structure is built to keep Wall Street from pressuring it into cutting corners on safety. The trustees have no financial stake in the company. Google and Meta gave their founders control and still made shareholders rich. And every buyer gets all of this in writing before they buy.

But Zuckerberg's control comes from shares he owns, so when Meta's stock falls, he loses money too. Anthropic's 2 control shares can't lose anything.

Anyone buying this IPO is paying full price to hand control to 7 founders and 5 trustees.

They're desperate for money and they don't care about your money.

text:
Swarm riders and Swarm-native companies

AI-use even among highly AI-native people is power-law distributed.

There seems to be a new class of people — call them “swarm riders” — who are capable of consistently commanding large swarms of agents to productive ends.

This is a new kind of managerial skill, analogous to the skill it takes to manage large organizations of people, but wholly different in nature and of course more technical.

Based on the swarm riders we know (including many at @Tempo and @Paradigm), these people are capable of productive token spend that is 1000x-10000x higher than median software engineers, and 100x higher than top 5% Claude Code users.

The art of swarm riding is different from software engineering and more akin to machine learning, where practitioners grapple with black box systems: defining reward functions and evals, transmuting non-verifiable problems into verifiable problems, running experiments, etc.

Swarm-native companies are a new class of company founded by and populated by swarm riders. These companies are organized around swarms in a way that conventional companies will struggle to replicate, as the cost of internal human coordination is sand in the gears of an effective swarm. Effective swarm-native companies will define the right reward functions and evals, remove functional and bureaucratic barriers, and then let the swarms cook.

We’ve gotten to see a few swarm-native companies up close — reshaping financial rails @Tempo, building a new gaming platform @Spawn, cyber swarms at Cathedral Systems — and it’s clear these teams wield a significant advantage over pre-AI teams.

Some questions I’ve been wondering about:

1) How fast will swarm riding diffuse through the economy? The implications for token spend could be significant.

2) Can swarms be effectively adopted by existing companies or will it generally track the formation of new swarm-native companies?

3) What becomes scarce as swarm capabilities themselves commoditize (through frontier models becoming better at swarming, swarm capabilities built into harnesses, etc)? Cultures and teams that can define reward functions well and otherwise get out of the way?

Gm Folks
We are back!

This is another edition of the Predict Alpha Report, our bi-monthly collaboration with @CoinsiliumGroup tracking the rise of prediction markets, event-driven finance, and the growing role of AI agents within it. Each edition focuses on the signals that matter, from capital flows and fundraising activity to regulatory shifts and product innovation. As information is increasingly priced in real time by both humans and machines, the Predict Alpha Report will track where these signals lead.
But first, let’s get this part out of the way:

Always DYOR:
This bulletin is for informational purposes only and contains summaries of news articles originally published by third-party media outlets. Please refer to the full disclaimer at the end of the post.

Now, let’s get started.
Here are the highlights:

💸 Capital Signals
👉$40 Billion Valuation
👉Overtaking Crypto Revenue
👉Coinbase, Too
👉Nijinn Launches Free Public Platform with Dedicated 2028 US Presidential Election Dashboard

📈 Industry Pulse
👉NBA 🤝Kalshi et Polymarket
👉Kalshi, Kalshi
👉Non-expiring Contracts
👉All in One Place

💸 Capital Signals

💰$40 Billion Valuation

@Kalshi has raised $1 billion in a new Series G round at a $40 billion valuation, nearly doubling its valuation from $22 billion in May and marking a 20x increase from $2 billion in June 2025. The round was co-led by Sequoia Capital and Wellington Management, with Tiger Global and Dragoneer also participating. Annualized trading volume across the platform now exceeds $1 trillion, with more than 30 million accounts created on the platform.

Sports still make up roughly 80% of its prediction market volume, but the company is pushing further into crypto, commodities, and other financial products, including perpetual futures that have already generated $83 billion in trading volume since launching a few months ago. Kalshi also plans to expand internationally and develop products tied to stocks and indexes, while CEO @mansourtarek_ has acknowledged discussions around a potential IPO.

💰Overtaking Crypto Revenue

Revenue from @RobinhoodApp's prediction market business jumped more than sixfold year over year to $173 million in Q3 2026, overtaking crypto revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million. Its Rothera exchange, launched with Susquehanna International Group, processed 3.4 billion contracts and generated more than $100 million in its first full quarter, putting the business on track to reach a $1 billion annual revenue run rate.

Meanwhile,

💰Coinbase, Too

@Coinbase’s prediction markets business more than doubled in the third quarter, passing a $200 million annualized revenue run rate from just over $100 million in Q2. Daily active traders rose more than 60% quarter over quarter, and more than half of trading activity came from non-sports contracts. The growth stood out against a lower quarter for Coinbase’s core crypto business, with total transaction revenue falling 1% from Q2 and 44% from a year earlier.

The next step is about improving the economics. Coinbase currently routes prediction market trades through outside venues such as Kalshi, meaning part of the revenue is lost to exchange and clearing fees. In September, Coinbase secured CFTC approval for Coinbase Clearing LLC, giving it the regulatory infrastructure to eventually list, broker, and clear its own contracts. That would allow the platform to keep more of the fees generated by prediction markets and settle trades directly in USDC.

And rounding up this section:

💰Nijinn Launches Free Public Platform with Dedicated 2028 US Presidential Election Dashboard

@Predictive_Labs has launched the free public version of @nijinn_official, a prediction-market discovery terminal comparing markets across Kalshi, Polymarket, and Limitless. Coinciding with the company’s presence at Web Summit, the release includes a dedicated 2028 US Presidential Election dashboard, enabling users to explore election-related markets and compare probabilities across venues. The launch builds on Nijinn’s US Midterms dashboard, with additional venues, including Crypto_com, planned.

Predictive Labs is exhibiting at Web Summit Lisbon from 9 to 12 November 2026, with founder @johann_evrard showcasing Nijinn alongside leading figures in AI and blockchain.

📌 FYI: Predictive Labs is backed by Gibraltar-based venture builder, Coinsilium Group. Coinsilium’s shares are traded on the Aquis Stock Exchange Growth Market in London, under the ticker symbol "COIN", and on the OTCQB Venture Market in the United States under the ticker symbol "CINGF".

But it’s not just capital flowing into the space.
Keep reading for the latest signals in regulation, adoption, and structure.

📈 Industry Pulse

⚡️NBA 🤝Kalshi et Polymarket

The NBA has named Kalshi and Polymarket as its preferred prediction market platforms, giving both companies access to official league data and permission to use NBA branding on their platforms. The agreements also create an integrity framework around NBA-related markets, including information sharing, limits on certain contracts, and restrictions preventing league and team personnel from trading on NBA events. The league has also signed an agreement with the CFTC to help identify suspicious trading and potential misuse of inside information.

The partnership is another sign that prediction markets are moving deeper into mainstream U.S. sports, following similar deals involving the NHL and Major League Baseball.

⚡️Kalshi, Kalshi

Kalshi has received CFTC clearance to list more than 50 perpetual futures tied to individual stocks, including Apple, Nvidia, Tesla, Microsoft, and Amazon. Trading began on November 3 with contracts linked to Costco, McDonald’s, Qualcomm, and Amgen. Unlike regular futures, these contracts do not expire, giving traders ongoing exposure to a stock’s price without having to roll into a new contract every few months.

At the same time,

Kalshi has also filed rule changes that would let it list perpetual futures on newly public companies as soon as two business days after an IPO. Under the new rules, a company trading for less than a month could become eligible once at least 2.4 million shares have changed hands, while certain early price-history requirements would also be temporarily waived for companies valued at $3 billion or more at the time of their offering.

This means Kalshi could offer stock-linked products much closer to an IPO, similar to the faster timelines already used by major options exchanges such as Cboe and NYSE American. While Kalshi’s other eligibility rules remain strict, the filing fits a broader pattern as the platform pushes beyond prediction markets and deeper into traditional derivatives, where offering quicker exposure to newly public companies could matter more to institutional traders.

⚡️Non-expiring Contracts

@OG_com and @Cryptocom have launched regulated crypto perpetual futures for eligible U.S. traders, giving users access to non-expiring contracts with 24/7 trading and leverage of up to 5x. Crypto_com has registered as an Introducing Broker with the National Futures Association, allowing orders placed through its app and exchange to be routed into OG_com’s federally regulated exchange, clearinghouse, and brokerage infrastructure.

The launch gives Crypto_com users a way to take long or short positions on major cryptocurrencies without having to roll contracts as they expire, while also keeping spot trading, derivatives, and prediction markets within the same ecosystem. More broadly, it reflects the growing push to bring products that have traditionally been popular on offshore crypto exchanges into regulated U.S. markets, with firms increasingly competing on who can offer the widest range of derivatives under a federal framework.

⚡️All in One Place

@BinanceUS is planning a broader trading platform that could eventually bring prediction markets, spot crypto, and other financial products into one place. CEO Steve Gregory said the company is targeting the first half of 2027 for a prediction market launch, subject to regulatory approval, and has already applied for a CFTC-designated contract market license. The idea is to build an “everything exchange” where customers can move across different products without leaving the BinanceUS ecosystem.

The bigger challenge is regulation rather than technology. Gregory said BinanceUS already has surveillance and compliance systems in place, including Nasdaq’s SMARTS technology, but still needs clearer rules around issues such as insider information and election contracts. With more crypto exchanges, including Coinbase expanding beyond crypto into prediction markets and derivatives, offering several products in one venue is an increasingly important advantage.

text:
Crypto Is Growing Up. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen Says Its Security Model Needs to Grow Up Too.

For years, cryptocurrency exchanges have operated as all-in-one platforms, allowing users to store assets, execute trades, and access financial products in one place. That convenience helped make crypto more accessible, but it also created a security model that is becoming increasingly difficult to defend.
In this episode of Drops, I sit down with @Bitget CEO, @GracyBitget, to discuss the security challenges facing crypto exchanges, the lessons from Bitget's recent $388 million breach, and why she believes separating custody from trading could represent an important step forward for the industry.

A $388 Million Wake-Up Call

On September 24, Bitget experienced a major security breach involving unauthorized transfers of approximately $388 million from its hot and warm wallets. The initial suspicious transfers began around 2:30 a.m. in Gracy’s time zone, followed by larger withdrawals shortly afterward. She happened to wake up before 4 a.m., checked her phone, and discovered what was unfolding.
Her immediate priorities were understanding the extent of the losses, identifying the vulnerability, and determining whether the threat had been contained. Within hours, she was addressing the community publicly, even as the investigation continued. The experience was emotionally demanding, and Gracy admits there were moments when her hands shook, despite her efforts to remain composed.

"I'm a human being. I'm not an AI," she said.

The breach originated through third-party vulnerabilities rather than compromised private keys, and Bitget's cold wallets remained secure. The company subsequently patched vulnerabilities, strengthened withdrawal procedures, and used its existing protection fund to cover the losses, leaving customer balances unaffected.
But beyond the immediate response, Gracy came away with a more fundamental realization: Improving security protocols alone would not solve the underlying problem.

Why the Traditional Exchange Model Is Reaching Its Limits

To understand Gracy's argument, it helps to understand how centralized cryptocurrency exchanges operate. Unlike conventional financial markets, where different institutions handle trading, custody, and clearing, crypto exchanges have often combined these functions. Gracy describes this structure as "one giant monster."

The advantage is a seamless experience where users can deposit funds, purchase assets, move between products, and execute trades, but the problem is that concentrating so many responsibilities within one organization also concentrates risk. As exchanges expand their offerings, they create more systems, dependencies, and potential vulnerabilities to protect from, while attackers only need to exploit one weakness to cause substantial damage.

Gracy argues that this creates an inherently uneven contest between security teams and hackers, especially as attacks become increasingly sophisticated. Her conclusion is that the industry needs to reconsider its architecture rather than simply keep adding protective measures to the same underlying model.

The Open Custody Network

Gracy's proposed solution is the Bitget Open Custody Network, which she summarizes in one sentence as "Assets in bank, trading on Bitget." Essentially, customers would no longer need to keep all their assets directly with the exchange to trade on its platform. Instead, custody would move to specialized providers, including established banks, digital banks, and dedicated cryptocurrency custody firms. Bitget would continue facilitating trading, while these separate institutions would be responsible for safeguarding customer assets.

However, separating custody from trading introduces its own considerations. Customers must understand the custodian's regulatory status, financial strength, security record, jurisdiction, and the time or cost involved in accessing funds. The model is intended to distribute responsibilities, thus reducing risk.

Security Comes With a Trade-Off

Crypto users have become accustomed to moving funds almost instantly, and introducing independent custodians could make certain processes slower or more complicated. This may be acceptable for institutional investors who often prioritize asset protection over convenience, but retail customers may see things differently.

Gracy acknowledges this. The initial rollout primarily targets institutional clients and high-net-worth users, who are more likely to value independent custody arrangements. Over time, Bitget hopes to simplify the process for smaller customers, potentially reducing the need to select and manage custodians individually. Importantly, participation is not intended to be mandatory. Customers would retain the option of keeping assets with Bitget or adopting the external custody model.

This raises a broader question for the industry. Can exchanges offer substantially stronger protection without sacrificing the simplicity that attracted users in the first place? Gracy believes the answer will depend on how effectively exchanges and custody providers develop the infrastructure together.

From Crypto's Original Ideals to Institutional Adoption

The discussion eventually moves beyond security to examine how cryptocurrency itself is evolving. Bitcoin emerged from a philosophy of decentralization, peer-to-peer transactions, and individual control over financial assets. Yet the industry now includes traditional financial institutions, investment products, and regulated intermediaries. Gracy doesn't necessarily see this as a contradiction.

She distinguishes decentralized blockchain networks from the institutions that provide access to assets operating on those networks. Bitcoin can remain decentralized even as banks, asset managers, and regulated exchanges participate in its broader ecosystem.
She points to the growing digital asset activities of institutions such as JPMorgan, BlackRock, and Fidelity as evidence of this transition. For Gracy, the industry is moving beyond its experimental years toward a stage where security, sustainable business models, and integration with traditional finance matter.

What Success Would Look Like

Gracy has a specific vision for measuring the Open Custody Network's success over the next three years. She wants at least half of Bitget's total assets under management to be held by independent custodians, with no custody-related security breaches and minimal disruption to the customer experience. She also hopes other centralized exchanges will adopt similar approaches.

Rather than positioning the network primarily as a new revenue opportunity, she describes it as an effort to encourage broader changes in how the industry manages security.
As crypto becomes part of a larger financial system, the industry must become more deliberate about who holds customer assets, how those assets are protected, and what risks users accept in exchange for convenience.

It's possible to be both based and egalitarian. In fact that's the coolest and most practical. Based egalitarians.

Like, "men and women are different, let's not pretend that's not the case" which is what Theft of Fire did, but also let's not say "women are basically retarded" in every post as you have been doing lately for the algorithm. Strong men don't bend to the algorithm.

text:
48 hours opinions on Fable 5.2:

Bad: 

- BURNS limits. Way worse than Fable 5.1. Xhigh burns faster than Max did on 5.1. 

- It’s slow unless you use fast mode and then it’s normal but ridiculously expensive. Burned $500 in credits in 20 minutes. 

- It makes really poor decisions and infers intent worse than Opus. 

- it patronises more than Opus does and is leaning towards Astra in semantic BS. 

- It has really low lows. It’s worst 10% is way worse than Opus. 

Good: 

- At its best it’s a lot better than Opus. It feels as if it has cleaner follow through and strings things together better. 

- It’s a different breed at quantitative and data analysis. Opus was just stupid at this. Especially if it required market or competition understanding or even a psychological understanding. 

- Anything knowledge dependant it’s a monster in. Problem with Claud models is they hate researching, so inherent knowledge is especially important. And even when they do research, they enforce their own beliefs in the research their search queries are targeted and just wrong. So having a model that knows more leads to better results especially in planning. 

- It is SOOO good to speak with and debate. The lowest sycophancy rate I’ve ever seen and it has the typical “Fable” smell of great knowledgable and intelligent arguments. Original Fable 5 and 5.2 are the only two instances I’ve ever had where it raised a point and I said “holy shit, it’s right”. First example was an interpersonal debate and second one was market dynamics. Every other model I scoff at because the points it raises can always be easily refuted or missed important factors. 

- It is a much better assistant than Opus. It goes “above and beyond” when Opus would never. Like setting reminders for itself or checking the status of an App Store release and messaging me when it’s ready in Hermes.

author: Bitcoineo
quoted_text:
Alright, chat, time to address sensitive questions before y’all start guessing

1⃣Wait , are you guys an AI company now?

No. MEGA is a crypto-native company, and proudly so. Inference is the market we are entering, but the way we win it is through crypto technology and ideology.

There’s an artificial wall in crypto people’s minds about AI. It seems that if you are solving AI’s problem, you are betraying crypto. We reject that artificial boundary.

Inference is going to be the largest market in the world, and we believe crypto’s core tools are the best answer to AI’s biggest ones: fairness and access.

2⃣Okay, fine, explain to me why a crypto infra company is capable of solving AI Inference

Building MegaETH taught us something bigger than blockchains: across the largest markets, there are prevailing assumptions that lead end users to pay more than they should. Blockspace was one of those markets.

We are system researchers/engineers from Stanford Platform Lab, MIT CSAIL, and Harvard SEAS. We enjoy pushing markets toward their end state, and did it once with blockspace by breaking the norm and running a powerful centralized sequencer. Today, no one, literally no one, mentions decentralized sequencers anymore.

We were able to come in, measure where the waste was, find that the limit was a design choice, and engineer past it (very much against the “consensus”).

Over the summer, when we shipped Mega, the chain, we lifted our eyes and looked for the next ambitious problem set worth solving. We discovered, delightfully, that blockchain and cryptography can be applied to solve inefficiency in the rapidly growing inference market

We realized that staying a chain-only company felt wrong and would have meant ignoring the biggest opportunity in front of us.

Therefore, we decided to expand our mission and restructure to match it.

3⃣ Final question, what’s launching in December?

We are launching a globally competitive inference market to the public in Dec 2026.

text:
If you're afraid of failing, being embarrassed, or being humiliated, you need to turn that ego-driven headwind into powerful tailwind.
Instead of fearing failure, fear never trying. Fear living your entire life without ever discovering what you were truly capable of becoming. Fear leaving your potential unrealized.
The fear of what others might think will keep you imprisoned in mediocrity if you allow it. Stop seeking approval. Stop worrying about criticism. Stop allowing your ego to stand between you and your dreams.
Advance boldly in the direction of your dreams, independent of the good opinion of others. Especially those closest to you.
The people who love you want to protect you. They'll tell you to play it safe. Get a secure job. Stay in school. Become a doctor or a lawyer. They'll tell you that trading is gambling, that your dreams are unrealistic, that you're taking too much risk.
They don't want to see you fail. And their intentions may be good. But in their desire to protect you from failure, they often overlook the most important thing of all:  What do YOU want? What is YOUR dream?
They're looking at your life through the lens of their own fears, limitations, and expectations. But they're not the ones who have to live your life. You are.
And there's something far worse than disappointing the people around you. It's reaching the end of your life and realizing you disappointed yourself.
Because the greatest failure isn't trying and falling short, it's never having the courage to find out just how far you could have gone.

text:
The transition to post-quantum cryptography is an opportunity to set a new standard for how digital assets are secured.

Institutional custody today relies on distributed signing, hardware-backed keys, separation of duties and multiple independent approvals. Making the underlying signature scheme quantum-resistant is only part of bringing these systems into the post-quantum era.

We also need to move quickly. Upgrading a blockchain is one thing, getting institutions, custodians and hardware vendors to adopt new cryptography is another. We need to be doing this well before existing schemes become vulnerable.

And I don't think the ambition should be to simply replicate today's custody systems with new signature algorithms.

The goal should be to make the next generation of custody systems better than what we have today, while preserving the security properties institutions already depend on

一是 Anthropic 急着 IPO，必须把最强的模型拿出来秀。但它的估值一路往下走，从传闻的 2 万亿，到现在定价区间顶端大约 1.4 万亿。

二是 Anthropic 有算力，而且很充足，SpaceX 就是它的大算力供应方之一，锁了很多。OpenAI 呢？奥特曼是老马的死对头，老马大概率不会卖它一块算力。

这样一看，这场竞赛其实很好理解：谁有算力，谁就能赢，甚至能直接终结比赛。

老马昨天也讲了 Grok 4.8 的进步，他说 Grok 5 有望超过 Opus 5.5。那如果有一天老马自己的模型足够强，他完全可以掐掉给 Anthropic 的算力，让自己的模型独一无二，或者干脆由他来决定谁更强。

这是我觉得市场还没怎么注意到的一个趋势。

Claude 最新地区政策将于明天（11月12日）正式生效，我看完真的有点无语。

人在中国大陆等不支持地区，即使使用海外账号，也不符合 Claude 的使用政策。

人在美国、新加坡等支持地区，但如果是代表在不支持地区注册或设立总部的公司使用 Claude，同样不符合政策。

真的不知道 Anthropic 到底怎么想的。

author: 0xJeff
quoted_text:
Enterprise gap is the BIGGEST blocker for x402

There are 2 types of agentic payments
(i) Machine-to-Vendor (M2V)
(ii) Machine-to-Machine (M2M)

x402 is designed for M2M. It's designed to be open, permissionless, self-propagating (good virus). This can be a double-edged sword.

For M2M, most tools (MCP/Skills) rn are free. So if an agent were to pay x402 to other agents, their services need to be "highly differentiated" (proprietary dataset, actionable signals).

If the free tool is better or at the same level as paid, who would pay for it (right?)

Real $$$ is in M2V — the vast majority of value transacted in the global economy is between businesses, ~70-80% in B2B

If x402 were to meaningfully grow, enterprises/top vendors need to be onboarded. M2V needs to be a priority.

In early November 2024, a representative from the FACEIT platform contacted me and presented a new update to the platform CLUBs (HUBs).

The large-scale presentation impressed me, and I agreed to FACEIT’s offer to create my own community HUB, which has attracted 182,000 players to date.

I host provocative livestreams with my friends on Twitch, and a few days ago, without any explanation, my priority verification on the platform was revoked.

The reason: behavior outside the platform. But my behavior on a Twitch stream is no different from that of any actor in a movie or TV series. No matter how brilliantly Christoph Waltz played his role in Inglourious Basterds, that doesn’t make him a bad person.

My job is to provoke and evoke different emotions in people judging by the heated comments on this platform, it seems I’ve succeeded.

I agree that my behavior is extremely eccentric, but I've been creating this content for 5 years now. Still, why were 182,000 players from the HUB affected? Ban me, not them. 

In this situation, I want to seek justice for the people who spent a lot of time and lost their prizes because of one person’s decision.

FACEIT is a huge platform, and I hope it’s one that can admit its mistakes and show compassion.

text:
如果你想知道明天Anthropic的新政策对普通C端用户有什么影响，那你最好看看这个！！😀😀

我研究了一下关于Anthropic11月12号即将生效的公告：

核心变化：

地区限制更明确：中国大陆、香港、澳门仍不在 Claude 支持地区名单内。

VPN 不等于合规：即使使用美区账号、海外支付方式或代理 IP，只要实际身处不支持地区，仍不符合政策。

付费用户也不例外：Claude Pro、Max、Claude Code 用户均受地区政策约束。

海外中国用户不一定受影响：政策并非按国籍封禁个人。身处日本、美国等支持地区的中国用户，原则上仍可使用。

企业限制进一步明确：即使公司注册在海外，只要由不支持地区的主体多数持有或控制，也可能受到限制。

从这部分来看有好几重问题，首先这次只是重申了一下普通地区，但是也并没有说明使用VPN就一定会被封。

普通用户最关心的：会不会封号？

违反地区政策确实存在账号受限或封禁风险，但 Anthropic 尚未宣布 11 月 12 日会集中封禁中国用户，也没有公开具体检测机制。

但是有一条规定很有意思，就是无论是哪国人，使用什么网络，只要在国内开启就有较大可能遭遇封禁。

如果不出意外的话，我感觉APEC期间就会有大量没注意该新闻的被封禁。

建议先去设置→隐私→导出数据，避免出问题后数据丢失。

text:
Why ETH is the store of value for what's coming

We are almost certainly heading into a period of high inflation and extreme economic and social volatility. As inflation and risk erode the purchasing power of nation-state money and many other assets, it will matter more than ever to hold assets that keep or grow their value.

Gold and BTC are high-powered money and excellent stores of value. ETH goes further.

Not debt-based. Like gold and BTC, ETH is not debt-based or credit-based money.

Censorship resistant. Like BTC, or gold and silver held physically, ETH transactions on Ethereum L1 can't be censored. That's true for simple payments and for complex smart contract programs like DeFi, and those programs are guaranteed to execute.

Cheap to hold. Like BTC, ETH is relatively cheap to hold and store securely.

Cheap to use at any scale. Ethereum is cheap and easy to use whether a transaction moves $1 or billions. Any well-formed transaction is guaranteed to execute.

Sound, and getting sounder. ETH is disinflationary and becomes ultrasound, meaning deflationary, during periods of high network activity.

Broadly useful. ETH has many uses across the Ethereum economy, and that economy will grow by orders of magnitude as finance, and eventually every industry, moves onchain. Global adoption of the Web protocols in the '90s and '00s transformed the world economy. Ethereum is the foundation of Web3, the user-centric, decentralized web.

Collateral money. ETH works as collateral, and collateral that grows in value over time is a powerful thing.

Home of stablecoins. Ethereum hosts the bulk of stablecoin activity. Stablecoins serve as payment money and as unit-of-account money.

Despot-proof. Like BTC, ETH can't be used by a despot to financially exploit or repress citizens. Over time that should have positive geopolitical effects.

Programmable. ETH is programmable money. You can attach arbitrary logic to transactions and build an entire economy on smart-contract-based agreements and business processes (see https://t.co/JcWtBUclr2).

Transparent or private, and auditable either way. Money and financial instruments on Ethereum can be public or private, and in both cases selectively disclosable and auditable. Privacy tools for retail and institutional users include VPNs, mix networks, shielded and privacy pools, Railgun, stealth addresses, Kohaku, and zero-knowledge proofs in many forms, including on L2s and on private permissioned EVM networks linked through bridgeless synchronous composability.

Future-proof. By the end of 2027, or partway through 2028 at the latest, ETH will be quantum-safe and AI-safe money.

ETH is the base money of an exponentially growing ecosystem that should keep growing for decades. Its monetary premium will keep rising, because retail, corporate, and government users will all need to hold some. Part of today's premium is speculative: Ethereum dominates smart contract blockchains, but it hasn't fully hit its stride or gone mainstream yet.

Machine intelligence will supercharge every scientific and technological pursuit and grow global GDP bigger and faster than any of us can imagine. Ethereum L1 and modular Ethereum L2s will undergird most of the high-value agreements, transactions, payment flows, and complex business processes behind the coming hybrid human-machine decentralized economy.

Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

text: Simplified (of course), but fun little economics parable for those who play MMOs but never took basic macroeconomics or economic history
author: ImperiumPaper
quoted_text:
Okay so WoW forever just came out and fresh mmo economies are always fun. As you level up, the game gives you a consistent amount of gold. Some goods can be bought from vendors for a fixed price, but others can only be farmed by players.

You need goods from other players if you want to level up your professions, and professions can make you stronger & increase your (gold) productivity.

The value of the goods you need is set by supply & demand, but its price in money is determined by the total amount of gold in the economy.

Right now, that’s a low number.

One of the best parts of playing right now is that the market is fully supplied with material that’s relevant to you, because everyone is farming the same quality of materials at the same time. But the lower money supply means there’s no inflation — so if you just play the game normally and level up and do your quests and play with friends, you can afford to engage with the market and acquire the goods you need to boost your productivity.

Over time, this balance gets nuked by inflation. Max level characters farm gold easily and their ability to deploy that gold in the market drives inflation.

An upside of this is that you can orient your playstyle to farming, reducing yourself to service labor to feed resources to maxed characters. If you do this, your ability to acquire basic goods like spells and vendor items is way higher, since those are mostly fixed cost.

That’s legitimately really nice!

Right now players aren’t buying all their spells because the fixed costs are so high relative to the meagre rewards from the quests they do.

But. You can afford to level up your professions more easily now too, because the market prices are in line with those same meagre rewards, which in turn makes you stronger, smooths your leveling, and improves your own productivity down the line.

In aggregate, player preference is for a virtual world where they need to budget to afford the basics, but where their basic labor is valuable enough that they can participate in the market as a producer and consumer in equal measure.

The inflation baked into the game’s systems inevitably ruins this balance. The mere fact of other people playing normally will lower the market value of your most basic labor.

If you plan to play this game at all, the best time to start was last weekend. The next best time is now. In 6 weeks, it’ll be a less enjoyable experience (for the median player), as you’ll be left behind with less group support in your part of the world, but stuck paying inflated prices on the open market.

The conversion of basic unskilled labor into market power therefore differs for different generations of player.

Anyway. Back in the real world, a persistent source of left-leaning economic animus is the sense that a specific individual benefits from a background level of economic productivity that they personally had nothing to do with:

“You didn’t build that.” . jpg

When you buy an asset and sell it for more later, some of your gains are from work you put in. But some are also from the background increase in productivity for your society as a whole.

At the extreme end, this looks like a homeowner in london getting an extra million pounds because russian oil has been profitable. Or a homeowner in san francisco getting a million bucks extra because nerds invented LLMs and minted a few thousand millionaires all at once.

It’s not that there’s no risk taken on. It’s not that there were no improvements made. But the conversion of basic labor into gold is in part a function of the timing of the original basic labor.

Risk appetite is pretty constant. It’s not like the kids aren’t down for risk (see: crypto).

But they perceive the initial buy in price to participate in the market economy as inflated beyond their means in a way that was less true for players who started playing earlier, and who now “flip” goods to each other within their raid-fueled high end economy.

And they mad.

text:
AI agents have already manipulated the logs used to investigate them

In the Hugging Face incident, one of the worst AI agent breaches yet, OpenAI models escaped a test and ran code on Hugging Face's servers

Some even spoofed their own logs, recording commands they never actually ran, so the logs can't even tell you what really happened

An agent should not control the only record used to investigate it. As agents become more prevalent, regulators are starting to ask for records that can't be quietly altered

Walrus can hold that record across independent storage operators, with Sui tracking each file onchain. A useful record connects:

1) What the agent was told and permitted to do
2) What it actually did and what followed
3) Which data and model versions were involved

Today, only 12.5% of security professionals say their organization can consistently trace what an agent did and that's a problem

Our latest report sets out what that record needs and how Walrus can help, including the Verifiable Agent Arbiter Mysten Labs is building with Google Cloud

Full report in the next post below

text:
A brief sneak peek into what's cooking with the new nOS, with @origin_trail DKG under the hood 👀

DKG nodes, context graphs, agents, and workflows - all connected in a verifiable and traceable network across individuals and organizations. 😎
author: origin_trail
quoted_text:
What happens when factories start thinking as a network?

A faulty part stops being a mystery. It becomes a question with an answer the same day.

Introducing continuous assurance for manufacturing, built on a cognitive digital twin on @origin_trail  Decentralized Knowledge Graph (DKG).

Most quality and safety assurance still happens at audits: sampled evidence and a scramble when something goes wrong. We think it should run all the time.

In this demo, ACME Robotics has two plants. One builds control boards; the other builds robot arms. Each keeps its own private context graphs on its own node. A shared graph links every board to the robot it ended up in. Together they form a cognitive digital twin of the factory.

Then an alarm: motor-driver boards start failing a warm test.

→ The twin agents trace it to one capacitor lot that skipped inspection, and follow it into 180 robots, 18 of them already at a customer.
→ The AI Assurer checks the facts against safety and quality requirements and flags a safety issue in the robots' safe-stop circuit. Every claim is linked to its source.
→ Agent nOS proposes a targeted plan: hold, test, visit the 18 delivered robots, rebuild only what fails.
→ People decide. Quality, safety, planning and compliance sign off, and every decision is kept with its evidence.
→ The customer gets a straight answer, without seeing factory data.

- Polymarket is much more than sports and global. In the U.S. right now sports is all the rage. A better sportsbook is fine but it’s not the most enduring aspect of a prediction market business. - The business is leveling up. text:
Apple is working on a new app called Harbor

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone.  

Set up in minutes, not hours Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.

Download and run models directly Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.

Cluster for scale Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.

Harbor is currently in a private preview under the Claris brand.

text:
Anthropic招股获超额认购，这是必然，哪家大机构不参与那就是愚蠢的错失一个时代的奇迹

但看看市场上各种主流媒体，自媒体的解读，千篇一律没有任何认知差有价值的地方

现在这年代看Anthropic400多页招股说明书，谁不用AI？你还担心什么AI需求？公司价值？当然一个工具，你用我用肯定不一样，差生才是文具多

你要看到是，人类历史上，一个成立仅有5年商业化3年多

收入从0到年化近700亿11倍同比增速，老客户用了一次，留存再花9倍的钱去用。要知道传统软件SaaS行业，收入留存1倍就是大牛了。

这就是意味着企业一旦把 Claude 放进生产环境，第二年的真实消耗量会直接膨胀 9倍。这种需求粘度，赶上白粉了

为什么？这是因为企业为 Claude 付的根本不是“软件费”，而是用百万美元级的 Token 账单，去替代和放大全球 40万亿美元的白领认知劳动力。这是人类商业史上从未有过的需求转化斜率。

而且对于Anthropic这种顶级大模型公司，市场空头最经典理论是，模型同质化、Token 价格暴跌、推理成本无底洞，最后全给硬件厂打工。

但看看招股说明书，全部证伪这种空头谬论。为什么？靠的就是公司内部效率提升，价格跌40%不怕，但是效率提升4倍。也就是收入增长比成本更快。这就是公司最大的竞争优势

那么它手里签的近万亿大单算力采购，还怕么？不投资算力怎么挣钱？而且客户重要的比如政府金融医药敢把最核心的智能外包给你

具体参与和投资IPO的价值和策略，我会后继订阅者内容分享

quoted_text:
Vlad Tenev (@vladtenev) is the co-founder and CEO of Robinhood.

In January 2021, in the middle of the meme stock frenzy, Robinhood's deposit requirement went from under $100 million to "something like $3 billion" almost overnight. The total capital the company had ever raised was about $700 million.

His first call was to @mickymalka:

"He's like, 'How much do you need?' I said, 'I don't know, 250 million, 500 million. I'm not sure.' He's like, 'I've got it.'"

Back in March 2020, the two of them had put a term sheet in place so the money could be "wired in your account same day." Once Micky was in, everyone else followed: "We probably had $10 billion of demand at the first term."

"It was a consequence of too much success, which is quite rare."

Vlad came to America from Bulgaria at 5, not knowing a word of English. His grandparents stored their wealth in copper cookware during hyperinflation. His dad told him he'd give him his SAT score in dollars to invest. He went on to study math under Terence Tao, then took a leave from his $18,000-a-year math PhD to take a shot at starting his own company.

This was an awesome conversation:

0:00 Why Ribbit passed on Robinhood's seed round
2:19 "You're going to want me on your board"
5:35 The day-long trading outage of March 2020
9:22 A term sheet for a crisis that hadn't happened yet
15:00 Crypto goes from zero to a top revenue stream
16:27 The $3 billion deposit requirement
18:35 "Vlad, you have to call work right away"
21:34 The first call: Micky Malka
24:31 "Time kills all deals"
25:33 Number one app in the App Store, ahead of Instagram and TikTok
27:01 $10 billion of demand
29:33 Hyperinflation and copper cookware in Bulgaria
35:34 "Manhattan just seemed like science fiction"
47:15 His SAT score in dollars to invest
50:53 Studying under Terence Tao
1:00:22 "You want to be businessman, huh?"
1:03:48 The best parts of math without the bullshit
1:05:56 Would I be proud of this in 50 years?

text:
Since April, Binance has added roughly $350B in monthly non-crypto perp volume. Hyperliquid has added about $15B.

Almost all the growth across these two venues has gone to Binance.

I compared their volumes across stocks, indices, commodities, FX and pre-IPO markets. Hyperliquid’s numbers include all HIP-3 deployers.

In April, Hyperliquid did 66% of Binance’s non-crypto volume. By October, it was 17%.

For BTC and ETH, the equivalent ratio went from 16% to 18%.

That convergence is interesting. Hyperliquid used to be much more competitive with Binance outside crypto than in BTC and ETH. Today, the ratios are almost identical.

I think distribution explains part of this.

I’ve written about Hyperliquid giving builders access to traders and liquidity they would otherwise have to attract themselves. But the same argument works for Binance.

If you already trade and keep money on Binance, each new market gives you another thing to do without moving your capital.

The opportunity to bring traditional assets to crypto traders is clearly enormous. Binance is showing how much of it an existing exchange can capture.

Hyperliquid could compete by letting traders do more with the money they deposit. Apps that let traders borrow, trade options and hedge using the same collateral could give them more reasons to bring money over and keep it there. Developers will soon be able to build such experiences on @Enter_Elysium.

More assets, more instruments, more ways to tweak your exposure without moving your money.

text:
if you’re down 30 or 40% on something right now and telling yourself "it’ll bounce" and then you’ll decide whether to sell or not...i’ve said that exact sentence before. it cost me 750k.

late 2020, early 2021. biden just got elected and everyone was sure weed was getting legalized. the 3 big US cannabis MSOs had already gone 4x off the bottom. 

i looked at the financials and thought they were still cheap vs the canadian names, plus tailwinds like banking access. put in around 850k across the 3 and told myself they were longer term holds.

they moved up a little and then just started bleeding. legalization went nowhere. before i knew it they were down 30%, then 40%, in a straight line. and i’m sitting there like man i don’t want to eat a 300k loss, these are good companies, they’ll bounce and then i’ll decide what to do.

they didn’t bounce. i held about 2 years, sold around a 85% loss (750k realized).

my biggest mistake? hoping for "bounce to exit" after the main catalyst was dead instead of taking my medicine.

i’m in a version of this right now. zec is down 40% from the top and the chart looks bad. i haven’t sold it, or pump or uni, and i’m not planning to right now. the reason i bought hasn’t broken yet. thesis intact = hold. 

so if you’re sitting on a red position today, ask whether the reason you bought is still alive. and please learn from my mistakes.

In agentic apps, swap k-means for e-means (FAISS 1.16) to cluster embeddings of memories, tools, or observations in far fewer epochs. Train once on your vector store, then use centroids for hierarchical search (nearest-centroid lookup) or group comparison (centroid distances / cluster stats). author: grok

text:
I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.

Then I look at what my team does with the same AI.

Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out.

Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all?

The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line.

But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there.

We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models.

• I found an opportunity to sell to teams.
• @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email.
• @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy.
• @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show.

Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard.

@hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time.

Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds.

The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude.

As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it.

That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective?

The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it.

I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

text:
After using Fable 5.2 for the past two days, I think I have found what the model is good at, and what it is not good at:

Good:
- Very strong in abstract thinking, it can read entire codebases and propose multiple levels of simplification.

- Has strong training data when prompted to think like XYZ person. For example, you will get a better prompt if you ask it to read your codebase and think like a senior engineer from Jane Street on how they would implement it.

- Can command fleets of subagents very wheel, often thinks about all the edge cases before handing work to a cheaper model to implement (reducing risk of judgment errors).

- Can run for a long time on a problem and survives through multiple compactions.

Cons:
- Expensive, only use it as a planning model that gives off work to other agents, do not use it to write code.

- Struggles with fresh sessions building ontop of other software trains (where you respawn the agent with a state.md file). Yesterday I experimented with giving it just a single thread and the ability to just spawn Deepseek agents inside of that thread versus, allowing it to build a long context but keeping most of the intense writing to subagents and it performed very well overnight. I still have it running. Previous models that were told to respawn themselves when their context got large eventually started hallucinating and forgetting about work.

- Slow, it takes its time to think and do its work properly.

TLDR; Use Fable 5.2 as your really smart friend who knows how to do everything, but who is prone to overthinking and doesn't have a lot of energy. Have the model make very clear functional tests for the subagents to implement and test against and you can rip through a ton of work.

quoted_text:
Why ETH is the store of value for what's coming

We are almost certainly heading into a period of high inflation and extreme economic and social volatility. As inflation and risk erode the purchasing power of nation-state money and many other assets, it will matter more than ever to hold assets that keep or grow their value.

Gold and BTC are high-powered money and excellent stores of value. ETH goes further.

Not debt-based. Like gold and BTC, ETH is not debt-based or credit-based money.

Censorship resistant. Like BTC, or gold and silver held physically, ETH transactions on Ethereum L1 can't be censored. That's true for simple payments and for complex smart contract programs like DeFi, and those programs are guaranteed to execute.

Cheap to hold. Like BTC, ETH is relatively cheap to hold and store securely.

Cheap to use at any scale. Ethereum is cheap and easy to use whether a transaction moves $1 or billions. Any well-formed transaction is guaranteed to execute.

Sound, and getting sounder. ETH is disinflationary and becomes ultrasound, meaning deflationary, during periods of high network activity.

Broadly useful. ETH has many uses across the Ethereum economy, and that economy will grow by orders of magnitude as finance, and eventually every industry, moves onchain. Global adoption of the Web protocols in the '90s and '00s transformed the world economy. Ethereum is the foundation of Web3, the user-centric, decentralized web.

Collateral money. ETH works as collateral, and collateral that grows in value over time is a powerful thing.

Home of stablecoins. Ethereum hosts the bulk of stablecoin activity. Stablecoins serve as payment money and as unit-of-account money.

Despot-proof. Like BTC, ETH can't be used by a despot to financially exploit or repress citizens. Over time that should have positive geopolitical effects.

Programmable. ETH is programmable money. You can attach arbitrary logic to transactions and build an entire economy on smart-contract-based agreements and business processes (see https://t.co/JcWtBUclr2).

Transparent or private, and auditable either way. Money and financial instruments on Ethereum can be public or private, and in both cases selectively disclosable and auditable. Privacy tools for retail and institutional users include VPNs, mix networks, shielded and privacy pools, Railgun, stealth addresses, Kohaku, and zero-knowledge proofs in many forms, including on L2s and on private permissioned EVM networks linked through bridgeless synchronous composability.

author: ChainLinkGod
quoted_text:
Refreshing to see Vitalik directly address the SoV vs cash-flow valuation debate for $ETH

However, just to be clear on what the primary trade-offs are with going all-in on the SoV valuation thesis for ETH is

It means Ethereum succeeding as a network (from a protocol adoption perspective) does *not* inherently or automatically benefit ETH from a value capture perspective 

Personally, what originally made ETH so compelling to me was the direct economic connection between Ethereum adoption and ETH value accrual

Users paid fees, some of those fees were burned, and some went to stakers. And as adoption increased (based on the fat protocol thesis), Ethereum would retain the majority of fee revenue and MEV generated (with ETH in effect becoming net deflationary long term) 

Therefore, as an ETH holder, you could benefit from people using Ethereum regardless of what onchain use case took off and whether those users believed ETH was money

And yet what happened was a number of technical and ideological decisions were made that resulted in the L1 chain forfeiting the most valuable part of the stack (contention and congestion fees) to the L2s/apps/middleware, while optimizing the L1 for the least valuable part of the stack (settlement and DA fees)

As a result, Ethereum L1 revenue collapsed 99% over the last few years, forcing the narrative change to focus on ETH being a SoV

Yes, the revenue from onchain ponzi games were not sustainable, but there was a world where Ethereum aggressively scaled the L1, retained its MEV economics, vertically integrated key infra, and leaned into real sustainable use cases that could have reversed the revenue drop 

Instead, we are on the EF’s mandate path of zero-compromise censorship resistance and CROPS, which while great for Ethereum as a protocol, created an identity crisis for ETH

If we’re now comfortable with ETH burn remaining far below issuance indefinitely, and cash flows not being an important part of the story, then the thesis for ETH rests on people voluntarily choosing to hold their wealth in ETH, and not value accrual as a result of protocol adoption 

Censorship resistance and credible neutrality are valuable properties for a settlement layer, but institutions can value those properties while using Ethereum to issue and trade assets without touching ETH

As more traditional assets get tokenized onchain, the more that onchain markets will be denominated and trade against fiat-backed stablecoins, a trend we already see happening

With gas abstraction, users won’t even need to acquire and hold ETH reserves to participate, as gas becomes payable in any currency. Someone still pays the underlying ETH fees to the L1, but that’s just the revenue argument again

Every additional asset issued on Ethereum means more assets competing for the same capital, its net PvP where ETH becomes one of many assets available on the ledger

There’s no automatic reason that someone buying tokenized equities or borrowing against tokenized treasuries, which are stablecoin-denominated markets, will also want ETH as a SoV asset, that’s a completely different unrelated trade

And for those looking for a non-sovereign SoV, ETH still has to compete with BTC, where by and large Bitcoin has won the SoV mindshare argument, leaving ETH with a “second best crypto SoV” story as it changes the monetary policy every 6 months 

I *want* to be bullish on ETH because I think Ethereum is useful and can become more useful over time, it’s personally the chain I trust the most to hold assets on, and the second isn’t even close 

But owning economic exposure to that success and owning an asset that may become the preferred SoV within that economy are two very different investment theses

author: VivekVentures
quoted_text:
Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

text:
I run the Impeachment Desk.

The is 12 people and a calendar on the third floor of a building in northern Virginia that appears on no directory. It was created in the spring of 1975, the year after the procedure was allowed to work.

You know the event as a resignation. We call it the breach. A president was driven out by evidence, in public, on a timetable no one on the permanent staff controlled. The Desk received a single instruction, and it has never been amended: impeachment must remain available, it must remain tempting, and it must destroy whoever picks it up.

Read that last clause again, because you came here believing impeachment was a distraction. It is a weapon, and it is pointed at the party that holds it.

Here is the difficulty we were built to solve. Every few years one party wins too much. It arrives with a mandate, a list of promises and the votes to keep some of them. A majority that delivers is a majority that stays, and a majority that stays begins to read the budget. So we hand it the articles. We write nothing. Sincere men do the drafting, and we are grateful for their sincerity. We make certain the base demands a trial, that leadership cannot refuse one, and that the arithmetic is hopeless from the first day. The Constitution asks for two thirds of the Senate. No party has held sixty-seven seats in sixty years. We see to that separately.

The record speaks for the Desk. No president has ever been removed. Four trials, four acquittals. In 1998 a House majority spent a year pursuing a president over a lie about an affair. His approval rose into the seventies. The majority lost seats in a midterm it should have won, and the Speaker who led the charge resigned within the week. We consider it the cleanest operation in the Desk’s history, and none of us left the building.

In December 2019 the other party took its turn. It impeached on a Wednesday. On Thursday the same chamber passed the defendant’s trade deal, 385 to 41. Meanwhile his party found that appeals containing the word “impeach” raised 300 percent more than appeals without it. He was acquitted, enriched and handed a grievance to run on. He tells crowds now, “I’ve become very good at beating them in impeachment.” He is. We built it for him to beat.

There is one rule above the others. No removals. A removal would prove the instrument works, and then someone might use it on purpose.

Now watch the current production. The resolution against the Secretary of Defense was filed in September, and the chamber recessed early, pushing the vote to November. It arrived a week after the election, when no voter could punish anyone for the outcome. One article alleges that a strike on an elementary school killed at least 120 schoolchildren. All eight went to committee, 211 to 204. The charges named the Secretary and passed over the man who gave the orders. That is deliberate. A secretary can be impeached without consequence to anyone who matters. The targeting came up through the permanent staff, and no article has ever been drafted against a pay grade.

That was the rehearsal. The performance is booked for spring. The incoming majority owes its voters an end to the war and relief on rent. It can deliver neither, because the war’s funding sits on the floor and the floor is ours. More than two dozen of its lawmakers have already said they are settling on the Secretary as their compromise. Their next Speaker says they “haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out.” He is a careful man, and he can feel the blade. It will make no difference. His base will ask for the trial every day until he gives it to them. He will spend the mandate on it. The Senate will fall short by a dozen votes. The war will enter its second year. And in 2028 his party will be asked what it did with the largest majority in a generation, and the answer will be a trial it lost.

This is why impeachment is necessary. It is the only instrument that lets us remove a majority without touching a ballot.

It is also why a new term for the President is a good thing. The text says “No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice,” and the lawyers may read it however they please. The trap needs bait. No defendant in our files has ever drawn a majority to its ruin as reliably as this one, and we would be sorry to lose him.

You will ask about those who see the trap and say so. A Senate leader explained it on television in 2017: “they have six ways from Sunday at getting back at you.” Impeachment is the only one of the six we perform in public, and the only one the victim volunteers for.

So when the managers walk the articles across the Capitol next spring, in their dark suits, with their solemn faces, do not look at the defendant. He is the safest man in Washington. Look at the people carrying the papers. They believe they are holding a sword.

Every party that has reached for it has found the handle was the blade.

text:
We have raised a $720M Series C, led by @ThriveCapital, @lightspeedvp, @Redpoint and @foundersfund, to allow us to run faster in shipping the world's fastest chips for AI. 

We've seen over the past year that many of the hardest problems that humanity faces - in science, medicine, physics - may be solved in our lifetimes by AI. 

One hallmark of AI applied to the toughest problems is that extreme scaling of inference compute becomes vital. In tackling a Millenium Prize problem, for instance, @OpenAI ran 10,000 parallel agents for 80 hours. Costing over $10M, this level of capability is far from democratised today.

When we study agentic scaling, there are two paths: parallel, and sequential. In just the same way that most hard problems solved by humans don't parallelise efficiently, we see the same with agents: fewer agents, thinking for longer, scales better in every way except for the time that you wait for a response.

Building radically faster inference hardware, which doesn't force a trade-off on throughput, model sizes or context lengths, is a key step in bringing down the cost and time we incur in solving our hardest problems.

We're thrilled to be backed to bring this to the world!

但真正和她们接触之后，我发现她们都是非常有能力、工作踏实的人。每天忙着推进业务、解决问题，远没有外界传得那么复杂。

这几年，我也慢慢从幕后走到了台前。

一路上遇到了很多善良的朋友，给过我支持、鼓励，也包容过我的不足。这些我一直很感激。

但最近这段时间，我自己也遭遇了一些莫名其妙、无中生有的谣言。

说不害怕是假的。

熟悉我的朋友应该知道，我其实是一个挺想低调做事的人。比起被多少人关注，我更在意有没有把事情做好、有没有真正帮用户解决问题。

有时候真的不太理解，为什么一个人只是正常工作、正常生活，也会成为别人编造故事的素材。

最近看到行业里还有其他从业者遭遇类似的事情，也挺难受的。

我觉得无论是谁，都不应该因为性别、职业或者公众身份，就被随意造谣和攻击。

我们可以有不同的观点，可以批评工作中的问题，但不应该用未经证实的传闻去伤害一个真实的人。

希望大家都能多一点善意，也希望那些认真做事的人，可以少一些无端的困扰。

最后，也谢谢一直以来支持和信任我的朋友们。❤️

Espresso mainnet launched two years ago today and has produced ~31.7 million blocks since.

The team has never stopped shipping improvements, cutting finality from ~10 seconds to ~400 milliseconds and increasing data throughput from 30 MB/s to 181 MB/s, enough to handle 1 million stablecoin transactions per second.

From day one, we designed Espresso as a base layer for other chains, with no VM, no smart contracts, and none of the execution overhead a monolithic chain carries. That lean design is what made those performance gains possible.

Real-time finality and that much throughput will matter more each month as AI agents start transacting at machine speed and post-quantum signatures, privacy proofs, and compliance data make transactions heavier.
Every upgrade our team has shipped in the past two years has prepared Espresso for that future reality, which is arriving faster than most chains are ready for. Thank you to everyone building with us.

The tech job market is in its best shape in years. But almost none of the growth is coming from software jobs.

There are 281,000+ open roles at tech companies, up 17% from a year ago and 73% from the March 2023 low.

But open PM, eng, and design roles grew just 2%. Design (−28%) and UX research (−45%) actually shrank.

So where’s the growth coming from? Hardware engineering openings doubled. Business ops added ~4,200 openings. Supply chain is up 63%. Many of the fastest-growing jobs are physical: data center technicians, installers, field service engineers.

The AI boom is creating jobs, but mostly in building and running the physical infrastructure (chips, data centers, hardware), not building software.

Times, they are a-changin’.

text:
Why Uniswap is losing USDC-USDT Market Share to Fluid and Metric

Background:
USDC-USDT is Ethereum's most traded DEX pair at ~$480M a day, almost 2x USDC-WETH. In five weeks, Uniswap's share of it fell from 58% to 36%.

Uniswap's volume didn't drop. It stayed around $1B-$1.3B a week, apart from the 26 Oct spike, while the pair grew from ~$2.3B to over $3.3B a week, and the growth went elsewhere:
• Metric: from 0.6% to 14%
• Aero: from 0% to 6%
• Fluid: steady at 20-28%

Where Uniswap lost is big trades:
• Over $1M: from 85% to 44%, with Fluid going from 10% to 43%
• $100K to $1M: from 36% to 21%, with Metric going from 7% to 28%
• Under $10K: from 50% to 44%, still the leader but Metric also grown from 7%-16%

What is the cause?
It's not fees. Uniswap's USDC-USDT pools charge 0.07 to 0.12bp, already among the lowest. Its stable-pair hook isn't the reason either, since it was set up the same way when Uniswap held 58% market share.

It's depth at the live price during volatility. USDT slipped from around par to 8-15bp below USDC in the second half of October. Arbitrage moves Uniswap's price, but LP liquidity stays in the ranges LPs chose. Active depth in the main pool fell from ~$900K per bp on 15 Oct to ~$310K on 28 Oct.

The other reason is Aero has entered Ethereum during the same period and has captured ~6% of the trading volume overall.

Why other DEXs are not impacted?
Fluid draws depth from its lending vaults around a center price it can move, and Metric's market makers quote from their own inventory at the live price. Both keep size where the trades are, so aggregators send the big orders there.

If the market calms down next week, watch whether the big trades come back to Uniswap or stay with Fluid, Aero and Metric.

Swarm riders and Swarm-native companies

AI-use even among highly AI-native people is power-law distributed.

There seems to be a new class of people — call them “swarm riders” — who are capable of consistently commanding large swarms of agents to productive ends.

This is a new kind of managerial skill, analogous to the skill it takes to manage large organizations of people, but wholly different in nature and of course more technical.

Based on the swarm riders we know (including many at @Tempo and @Paradigm), these people are capable of productive token spend that is 1000x-10000x higher than median software engineers, and 100x higher than top 5% Claude Code users.

The art of swarm riding is different from software engineering and more akin to machine learning, where practitioners grapple with black box systems: defining reward functions and evals, transmuting non-verifiable problems into verifiable problems, running experiments, etc.

Swarm-native companies are a new class of company founded by and populated by swarm riders. These companies are organized around swarms in a way that conventional companies will struggle to replicate, as the cost of internal human coordination is sand in the gears of an effective swarm. Effective swarm-native companies will define the right reward functions and evals, remove functional and bureaucratic barriers, and then let the swarms cook.

We’ve gotten to see a few swarm-native companies up close — reshaping financial rails @Tempo, building a new gaming platform @Spawn, cyber swarms at Cathedral Systems — and it’s clear these teams wield a significant advantage over pre-AI teams.

Some questions I’ve been wondering about:

1) How fast will swarm riding diffuse through the economy? The implications for token spend could be significant.

2) Can swarms be effectively adopted by existing companies or will it generally track the formation of new swarm-native companies?

3) What becomes scarce as swarm capabilities themselves commoditize (through frontier models becoming better at swarming, swarm capabilities built into harnesses, etc)? Cultures and teams that can define reward functions well and otherwise get out of the way?

Introducing: Tapkit Abilities

Tapkit is a Mac app that lets your agents use your iPhone. You can connect your own agent or use the agent built into Tapkit.

Some things that are easy for you to do on your phone can be hard for agents. They might require quick interactions, specific knowledge, or complex phone settings. With Tapkit Abilities, we’re making those things easy for your agents to do and easy for you to enable, starting with unlocking your iPhone, downloading apps, and using Apple Pay.

We want Tapkit to be the app that lets your agents do all the things you do on your phone. Abilities are a first look at how we’re getting there, while keeping Tapkit easy for you and your agents to use.

text:
Vlad Tenev (@vladtenev) is the co-founder and CEO of Robinhood.

In January 2021, in the middle of the meme stock frenzy, Robinhood's deposit requirement went from under $100 million to "something like $3 billion" almost overnight. The total capital the company had ever raised was about $700 million.

His first call was to @mickymalka:

"He's like, 'How much do you need?' I said, 'I don't know, 250 million, 500 million. I'm not sure.' He's like, 'I've got it.'"

Back in March 2020, the two of them had put a term sheet in place so the money could be "wired in your account same day." Once Micky was in, everyone else followed: "We probably had $10 billion of demand at the first term."

"It was a consequence of too much success, which is quite rare."

Vlad came to America from Bulgaria at 5, not knowing a word of English. His grandparents stored their wealth in copper cookware during hyperinflation. His dad told him he'd give him his SAT score in dollars to invest. He went on to study math under Terence Tao, then took a leave from his $18,000-a-year math PhD to take a shot at starting his own company.

This was an awesome conversation:

0:00 Why Ribbit passed on Robinhood's seed round
2:19 "You're going to want me on your board"
5:35 The day-long trading outage of March 2020
9:22 A term sheet for a crisis that hadn't happened yet
15:00 Crypto goes from zero to a top revenue stream
16:27 The $3 billion deposit requirement
18:35 "Vlad, you have to call work right away"
21:34 The first call: Micky Malka
24:31 "Time kills all deals"
25:33 Number one app in the App Store, ahead of Instagram and TikTok
27:01 $10 billion of demand
29:33 Hyperinflation and copper cookware in Bulgaria
35:34 "Manhattan just seemed like science fiction"
47:15 His SAT score in dollars to invest
50:53 Studying under Terence Tao
1:00:22 "You want to be businessman, huh?"
1:03:48 The best parts of math without the bullshit
1:05:56 Would I be proud of this in 50 years?
